You are composing the Round 10 revision of a research idea JSON. I will give you the complete original JSON and precise instructions for what to add. Your job is to output the complete revised JSON with ALL fields filled exactly as in the original, plus the additions described below. Do not summarize, truncate, or paraphrase existing content — preserve every sentence verbatim and insert the new content at the specified locations.

## Changes to make

### 1. In `core_problem` field
After the sentence ending "...a finding with direct generalization to any retrieval system using LLM-inferred labels for query routing." — ADD this sentence:

"Section 5 of the paper derives analytically the condition under which hard partitioning is net-positive: with X = classifier accuracy, Z = relative repair improvement for correctly-classified instances, and W = relative degradation for misclassified instances, the breakeven threshold is X* = W/(Z+W); this bound is domain-agnostic and converts the generalization claim from assertion to principled result."

### 2. In `opportunity` field
After the sentence ending "...PatchRecall (arXiv 2604.10481, April 2026) introduces history-based retrieval for file-level localization on SWE-bench — complementary scope." — ADD:

"RouterRetriever (AAAI 2025, arXiv:2409.02685) provides cross-domain empirical grounding for the retrieval-routing partition hypothesis: routing queries to domain-specific expert embedding models outperforms a unified retrieval model by +2.1 nDCG@10 on BEIR, with instance-level oracle routing achieving 57.6 vs. actual routing at 49.6 nDCG@10 — an 8.0-point gap that quantifies the cost of imperfect routing, the open-domain IR analog of FTCR's W% decomposition. RouterRetriever uses similarity-to-pilot-embeddings routing rather than an LLM classifier; FTCR's X%/Z%/W% measurements extend the oracle-vs-actual routing gap analysis to classifier-based routing in code repair, filling an empirical gap that RouterRetriever, M-RAG, and ReCode leave open across their respective domains."

### 3. In `approach` field
After the paragraph beginning "NLP Lead Contribution: LLM Label Quality and Downstream Retrieval Impact." and ending "...This generalizes beyond code repair to any system that uses LLM-generated labels to route queries into type-specific retrieval pools." — ADD a new paragraph:

"Analytical Derivation: Condition for Hard Partitioning to Dominate Soft Retrieval. Let X ∈ [0,1] denote classifier accuracy (probability of correct type assignment at the minor-type level), Z > 0 the relative repair improvement for correctly-classified instances under hard type-partitioned retrieval compared to the soft joint-embedding baseline, and W > 0 the relative repair degradation for misclassified instances. The expected repair benefit of hard partitioning over the soft baseline is E[ΔRepair] = X·Z − (1−X)·W. Setting E[ΔRepair] > 0 and solving yields the breakeven classifier accuracy threshold: X* = W/(Z+W) = 1/(1 + Z/W). Hard partitioning is net-positive if and only if X > X*. Three properties of this bound are immediately applicable: (i) when Z = W (symmetric benefit and cost), X* = 0.5 — any above-chance classifier yields net benefit; (ii) when Z > W (correct routing provides larger gain than misrouting costs), X* < 0.5; (iii) when Z < W, X* > 0.5, requiring a substantially accurate classifier. This threshold is domain-agnostic and converts the generalization claim from assertion to principled result: given any pilot measurement of Z and W, a practitioner can predict whether hard partitioning is net-beneficial without a full ablation. The magnitude of Z is governed by within-type patch coherence, quantified as Δc = c_in − c_out, where c_in (c_out) is the mean cosine similarity between query bugs and retrieved patches of the same (different) type under the text-embedding-3-large encoder. When Δc is large, the encoder already separates types in embedding space and soft retrieval implicitly type-matches, so Z → 0 and hard partitioning adds little; when Δc is small, soft retrieval fails to type-match and hard partitioning maximally benefits. FTCR's embedding experiments measure Δc as a byproduct of the intra-corpus ablation, empirically connecting within-type patch coherence to the magnitude of Z and W — and therefore to X*. RouterRetriever (AAAI 2025, arXiv:2409.02685) provides cross-domain empirical grounding: routing queries to domain-specific expert embedding models outperforms a unified retrieval model by +2.1 nDCG@10 on BEIR, with instance-level oracle routing at 57.6 vs. actual routing at 49.6 nDCG@10 — an 8.0-point gap that is the open-domain IR analog of FTCR's W% cost-of-misrouting decomposition. The hierarchical structure of the DebugBench taxonomy provides a natural bound on W: within-major misclassifications (e.g., null-dereference classified as undefined-method, both Reference type) have lower W than cross-major misclassifications (null-dereference classified as missing-colon, Syntax type), because within-major types share fix-operator families. The confidence-gated fallback — which reverts to soft retrieval below threshold τ — is the system-level implementation of the X* insight: for instances where the classifier's top-class probability signals likely misclassification, falling back to soft retrieval recovers the W cost."

### 4. In `approach` field, in the "Practical Utility" paragraph
After the sentence ending "...Standalone evaluation isolates the retrieval hypothesis cleanly." — ADD:

"To make the pipeline compounding argument concrete: ReinFix's retrieval component contributes +38 bugs on Defects4J V2.0 over the no-retrieval baseline, quantifying retrieval's marginal value. If FTCR achieves a relative Z% improvement over ReinFix-style retrieval for correctly-classified instances (fraction X of queries), switching to FTCR retrieval in a combined pipeline would add approximately 38 × X × Z additional bugs through retrieval alone — at X=0.65 and Z=0.10 (conservative), that yields ~2.5 additional bugs from retrieval, compounding further in a DynaFix-style iterative loop where better initial patches reduce iterations required (DynaFix's NeurIPS 2025 iterative loop feeds execution feedback back to the LLM, so a more fix-template-aligned initial patch reduces the number of failed iterations before convergence). This frames FTCR as a drop-in retrieval module upgrade for any pipeline that separates retrieval and generation components, with marginal pipeline gain ≈ Z × (retrieval_contribution/total_pipeline_rate)."

### 5. In `resource_estimate.auto_research.day_by_day_schedule` field
In the "Day 4–6" entry, after "Pre-drafted paper skeleton (introduction, related work, method) during this window to reduce Day 13–15 writing pressure." — ADD:

"The skeleton uses a five-section modular structure — (1) Introduction: the threshold question; (2) Analytical Framework: derivation of X* = W/(Z+W), identical regardless of experimental outcome; (3) Experimental Setup: identical regardless of outcome; (4) Results: X%/Y%/Z%/W% measurements with tables; (5) Discussion: interprets measured X% relative to the derived threshold X* = W/(Z+W) — so that both outcome branches (Z% > 0, confirming hard partitioning is net-beneficial above the threshold, or Z% ≤ 0, documenting that X% falls below X* and constituting a failure-mode finding) require only Discussion-section reframing without restructuring Introduction, Method, or Results. This eliminates the wholesale-rewrite risk from the two-day writing window."

### 6. In `key_references` field
ADD a new entry at the end of the list:

"RouterRetriever: Routing over a Mixture of Expert Embedding Models (AAAI 2025, arXiv:2409.02685, Lee et al.) [cross-domain empirical support for the retrieval-routing partition hypothesis; routing queries to domain-specific expert embedding models outperforms a unified MSMARCO-trained model by +2.1 nDCG@10 and multi-task models by +3.2 on BEIR; instance-level oracle routing achieves 57.6 vs. actual routing at 49.6 nDCG@10 — an 8.0-point oracle-vs-actual gap that is the open-domain IR analog of FTCR's (Z%, W%) cost-of-misrouting decomposition; RouterRetriever uses similarity-to-pilot-embeddings routing (not an LLM classifier), so FTCR's X%/Z%/W% measurements extend the oracle-vs-actual gap analysis to classifier-based routing in code repair; cite in Analytical Derivation section as cross-domain empirical grounding for the partitioning theorem]"

### 7. In `description` field
After the sentence ending "...These quantities are a direct empirical answer..." ADD:

"Section 5 derives analytically the breakeven classifier accuracy threshold X* = W/(Z+W) — the condition under which hard partitioning is net-positive — converting the generalization claim from assertion to a domain-agnostic principled result, with RouterRetriever (AAAI 2025, arXiv:2409.02685) providing cross-domain IR empirical grounding."

### 8. Set `change_type` field to "minor"

{
  "title": "Failure-Type-Conditioned Retrieval Augmentation for Repository Repair",
  "project_name": "failure_type_rag_repair",
  "source": "web_research",
  "level": "solid",
  "core_problem": "The lead empirical question — tractable because DebugBench provides oracle ground-truth labels for 4,253 instances organized in a 4-major/18-minor hierarchical taxonomy — is: how accurately can a few-shot LLM assign semantic bug type labels from the 18 minor sub-categories, and does that label accuracy determine whether hard categorical retrieval index partitioning outperforms soft root-cause-augmented retrieval (ReinFix, ICSE 2026) for cross-repository fix template transfer? Prior work (arXiv:2407.06153, EMNLP 2024) established a baseline accuracy floor: fully-automated zero-shot GPT-4 classification of fine-grained bug types achieves only ~37% at the secondary level and ~5% at the tertiary level on a custom 3-primary/10-secondary taxonomy over LLM-generated code. However, that same study showed AI-assisted annotation (GPT-4 suggestions + human demonstrations) reaches 91.6% tertiary accuracy — an 18× improvement over zero-shot at the tertiary level — demonstrating that structured demonstration examples dramatically improve LLM classification performance. This frames FTCR's X% measurement as a direct empirical test of the hypothesis: 'does task-specific few-shot prompting with DebugBench-aligned demonstration examples, applied to a purpose-built 4-major/18-minor taxonomy of natural repository bugs, overcome the documented zero-shot accuracy floor in general LLM bug classification?' The practical stakes are high and symmetric: if X% ≈ 35% (the zero-shot floor), hard partitioning hurts on average and the paper's conclusion is a documented negative; if X% ≥ 65% (the few-shot hypothesis), correctly-classified instances driving Z% substantially outnumber misclassified instances driving W%, and type-conditioned retrieval is net-beneficial. Either outcome is a publishable finding with direct generalization to any retrieval system using LLM-inferred labels for query routing.\n\nThis frames FTCR as an empirical study of LLM-generated categorical label quality and its downstream retrieval impact, yielding four falsifiable quantities: (X%) few-shot classifier accuracy vs. DebugBench ground-truth oracle labels at the minor-type level, with major-type aggregation as a secondary result; (Y%) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer accuracy to Java bugs (n=56 pairs, reported as a preliminary cross-lingual signal with 95% CI for the proportion estimate); (Z%) repair improvement for correctly-classified high-confidence instances under hard type-partitioned retrieval vs. the soft baseline; (W%) repair degradation for misclassified instances. Together these characterize when hard categorical type conditioning helps and when it hurts — a finding with direct generalization to any retrieval system using LLM-inferred labels.\n\nRetrieval-augmented repair systems fall into two camps: code-text-similarity retrieval (RAP-Gen, RELREPAIR) and soft root-cause-augmented retrieval (ReinFix, ICSE 2026), which concatenates an LLM-generated free-text root-cause description with the buggy code into a unified embedding space using text-embedding-3-large. Neither approach exploits the structural regularity that bugs of the same semantic TYPE — null dereference, off-by-one, API misuse, type mismatch, concurrency — share fix templates even when code looks syntactically dissimilar. InferFix (ESEC/FSE 2023, arXiv:2303.07263) establishes that type-conditioned retrieval benefits code repair: its Retriever uses contrastive learning where same-type bug-fix pairs are training positives and different-type pairs are negatives (type from Infer static analysis), and at retrieval time filters candidates to same-type fixes; however, InferFix requires running the Infer static analyzer on each query bug — applicable only to bugs Infer can detect, using Infer-specific diagnostic categories rather than a general natural-bug taxonomy. TypeRepair (SQJ 2026, Zhang et al.) validates that defect type identification improves LLM-based repair, but its mechanism is type-conditioned within-project context selection and type-specific prompt guidance — not retrieval from an external cross-repository fix corpus. The open question is therefore two-fold: (1) whether LLM-inferred type labels can substitute for Infer-derived labels to enable type-conditioned retrieval for general natural bugs not addressable by static analysis (the X%/Y% question vs. InferFix); and (2) whether hard categorical type partitioning of the retrieval index outperforms ReinFix's soft semantic root-cause augmentation for cross-repository fix transfer (the Z%/W% question). An independent empirical finding (Gu et al., ICSE 2026, arXiv 2503.20589) strengthens the motivation: similar code snippet retrieval degrades code generation performance by up to 15%, while contextual and structured knowledge retrieval helps. Type partitioning ensures retrieved patches share semantic repair structure (the fix operation) rather than superficial syntactic similarity, precisely avoiding the degradation trap Gu et al. identify. Two methodological challenges discipline the comparison and become analytical contributions when addressed directly: (1) corpus sparsity — a natural bug-fix corpus of ~3,050 pairs across the 14 single-fault minor types (Syntax×7, Reference×4, Logic×4; the Multiple Bugs sub-types are excluded from the fix-template corpus as multi-fault commits are rare and represent a different repair regime) yields approximately ~217 pairs per minor type on average for the full Python+Java corpus; for Java-only ablations (~559 pairs across ~14 types, ~40 per type), types with fewer than 30 instances are merged within the same major category (e.g., rare Syntax sub-types merged within Syntax; rare Logic sub-types merged within Logic — never across major categories); and (2) classifier error propagation — when an incoming bug is misclassified, hard partitioning underperforms soft retrieval for those instances, making the performance gap conditional on classifier confidence. Addressing both challenges — by measuring classifier accuracy against DebugBench's ground-truth labels and adding a confidence-gated fallback — turns potential weaknesses into the core empirical variables (Z% and W%) that define the paper's scientific contribution.",
  "opportunity": "ReCode (CIKM 2025, arXiv 2509.02330) demonstrates algorithm-type-aware retrieval in competitive programming but is explicitly scoped to algorithmic tags (greedy, DP, graph). InferFix (ESEC/FSE 2023, arXiv:2303.07263) is the earliest type-conditioned cross-repository retrieval system for code repair: its Retriever is pretrained via contrastive learning where same-type bug-fix pairs are training positives and different-type pairs are negatives (type labels from Infer static analysis), and at retrieval time filters candidates to same-type fixes using Infer-derived labels. The encoder itself encodes only the buggy code as a dense vector — type structures the contrastive training pairs but is not an explicit encoder input; the retriever learns type-correlated semantic similarity. InferFix achieves 76.8% top-1 accuracy on Java and 65.6% on C#. Three properties distinguish InferFix from FTCR: (a) Type label acquisition — InferFix requires running the Infer static analyzer on each query bug to obtain its type label; only bugs Infer can detect are addressable; FTCR uses few-shot LLM classification, requiring no static analysis tooling and covering any natural bug that Infer cannot or would not detect; (b) Taxonomy scope — InferFix uses Infer-specific diagnostic IDs (null dereferences, resource leaks, thread-safety violations), not the 4-major/18-minor natural-bug taxonomy aligned with DebugBench (4 major categories: Syntax with 7 sub-types, Reference with 4 sub-types, Logic with 4 sub-types, Multiple Bugs with 3 sub-types); (c) Corpus — InferFix uses InferredBugs (Java/C# repos where Infer detected bugs); FTCR uses natural bug-fix pairs from issue trackers and CI logs. This establishes a documented accuracy floor for zero-shot general classification and directly motivates FTCR's X%/Y% measurements as the key empirical test: do few-shot demonstrations with DebugBench-specific examples bridge the 37%→91% gap for natural repository bugs without human-in-the-loop verification? InferFix validates that type-conditioned retrieval works (supporting FTCR's hypothesis) while leaving the LLM-label-quality-vs-retrieval-effectiveness question entirely unanswered. ReinFix (ICSE 2026, arXiv 2506.23100) advances toward root-cause-conditioned retrieval for real-world repositories, showing +32 bugs fixed on Defects4J V1.2 and +38 on V2.0, but its mechanism — LLM-generated free-text root-cause descriptions embedded jointly with buggy code in one unified vector database using text-embedding-3-large — is a soft, continuous approach without type-level partitioning. SWE-Exp (arXiv 2507.23361, revised February 2026) introduces an experience bank that retrieves the top N=10 issues 'most relevant in terms of error type' using soft cosine similarity over (issue-type + description) embeddings encoded by Multilingual-E5-Large; it stores distilled modification strategies rather than concrete fix patches, operates as a fully agentic pipeline, and is scoped to Python. SWE-Exp's type signal is a soft retrieval-time metadata feature, not a hard index-construction partition; FTCR's structural departure is to partition the retrieval corpus into discrete type sub-indices before any query is issued, enabling retrieval-pool precision rather than post-hoc reranking. TypeRepair (SQJ 2026, Zhang et al., doi:10.1007/s11219-026-09751-w) independently validates that defect type identification improves LLM-based repair: its 4-stage pipeline (localization → type ID → context selection → patch generation) with 10 defect types achieves 272% improvement over GPT-3.5 on Defects4J V1.2/V2.0 and QuixBugs. Crucially, TypeRepair's context selection stage uses the identified type to select within-project code context and generate type-specific repair guidance for the LLM prompt — it retrieves no external cross-repository fix corpus. TypeRepair is Java-only; FTCR extends type-conditioned repair to C++/Java/Python with cross-repository retrieval of ~3,050 historical fix patches. TypeRepair establishes that type conditioning matters (validating FTCR's hypothesis) while leaving hard-vs-soft type-partitioned cross-repo retrieval entirely unexplored. Gu et al. (ICSE 2026, arXiv 2503.20589) provide independent empirical motivation: retrieving syntactically similar code snippets degrades repository-level code generation by up to 15% on CoderEval and RepoExec, while contextual code and API information significantly helps. Fix patches retrieved by type partition share the semantic repair operation (null-check insertion, bounds guard, API substitution), while patches retrieved by surface code similarity may look similar yet represent different fix operators, concentrating exactly the noise Gu et al. identify. DynaFix (arXiv 2512.24635) subsequently surpasses ReinFix on Defects4J V2.0 using execution-level dynamic information and iterative repair, confirming that retrieval strategy and execution-level augmentation are independently improvable axes; FTCR operates on the retrieval strategy axis. RetypeR (ICSME 2024) applies type-specific retrieval but only for Python type errors (one narrow subcategory). The untested hypothesis is that hard categorical type partitioning — classify the incoming failure into one of the 18 minor semantic sub-types, then retrieve only from the type-matched sub-corpus — yields better precision in retrieving transferable fix templates than ReinFix's joint root-cause embedding, because bugs within a type share syntactic fix motifs that bugs with merely similar embeddings but different repair operators do not. DebugBench's 4-major/18-minor hierarchical taxonomy uniquely provides 4,253 instances with ground-truth type annotations across C++, Java, and Python (organized as: Syntax/7 sub-types, Reference/4, Logic/4, Multiple Bugs/3), enabling direct classifier calibration at the minor-type level and turning error propagation from a latent risk into the paper's core measurable variable. The confidence-gated hybrid has principled precedent in CRAG (Yan et al., 2024; arXiv:2401.15884). M-RAG (ACL 2024, arXiv 2405.16420) validates that partition-based retrieval consistently outperforms single-store retrieval across NLP tasks, providing domain-general support for the partition hypothesis. PatchRecall (arXiv 2604.10481, April 2026) introduces history-based retrieval for file-level localization on SWE-bench — complementary scope. The APR survey (arXiv 2506.23749) reviews 63+ systems with no type-partitioned cross-language retrieval system identified.",

InferFix achieves 76.8% top-1 accuracy on Java and 65.6% on C#, outperforming LLM baselines by 11–55%. The scientific question InferFix leaves open — and FTCR directly tests — is whether LLM-inferred type labels achieve sufficient accuracy (X%) to enable type-conditioned retrieval that is effective for general natural bugs, and at what accuracy threshold does type-conditioned retrieval outperform soft embedding baselines (Z% > 0%, W% < Z%). What's Wrong with Your Code Generated by Large Language Models (arXiv:2407.06153, EMNLP 2024) provides the accuracy baseline that FTCR's X% must be measured against: fully automated zero-shot GPT-4 classification achieves ~37% secondary-level and ~5% tertiary-level accuracy on a custom 3-primary/10-secondary taxonomy over LLM-generated code (HumanEval+, MBPP+, APPS+); however, AI-assisted annotation with structured GPT-4 demonstrations reaches 91.6% tertiary accuracy. FTCR's X% measurement directly tests whether these three factors together are sufficient to bridge the documented zero-shot accuracy floor — framing X% as an empirical NLP finding rather than an implementation detail. ReinFix (arXiv 2506.23100, ICSE 2026) is the closest prior work and primary baseline: it uses an LLM to generate a free-text root-cause description per bug, then embeds (buggy_code + root_cause_text) as a single concatenated string into a unified vector database using text-embedding-3-large, built from 100K samples of the TRANSFER corpus (1M bug-fix pairs). Retrieval is by cosine similarity over this joint embedding — no type-level partitioning. Corpus quality confound: comparisons against published ReinFix results conflate two variables simultaneously — retrieval architecture (soft joint embedding vs. hard type partition) and corpus quality (100K TRANSFER synthetic pairs vs. 3,050 natural bug-fix pairs from issue trackers and CI logs). Intra-corpus ablations (FTCR vs. re-implemented ReinFix-style baseline on the same 3,050-pair natural corpus using the same text-embedding-3-large encoder) test the partitioning hypothesis cleanly and isolate architecture as the variable. Absolute comparisons against published ReinFix numbers reflect both architecture and corpus quality differences simultaneously and are presented explicitly as such; they are not used to claim a clean head-to-head win on architecture alone. SWE-Exp (arXiv 2507.23361, revised February 2026) retrieves top N=10 issues 'most relevant in terms of error type' using soft cosine similarity over (issue-type + description) embeddings (Multilingual-E5-Large), achieving 73.0% on SWE-bench Verified with Claude 4 Sonnet in a fully agentic Python-only pipeline. Three design differences: (1) soft vs. hard — SWE-Exp uses type as retrieval-time embedding metadata; FTCR partitions at index-construction time; (2) retrieved artifact — SWE-Exp stores distilled modification strategies; FTCR retrieves concrete fix patches; (3) scope — SWE-Exp is agentic and Python-only; FTCR covers C++/Java/Python in retrieval-only mode. TypeRepair (SQJ 2026, Zhang et al., doi:10.1007/s11219-026-09751-w) applies a 4-stage pipeline with 10 defect types on Defects4J V1.2/V2.0 and QuixBugs, achieving 272% improvement over GPT-3.5. TypeRepair's context selection stage conditions on the identified defect type to select within-project code context and provide type-specific repair guidance — it does not retrieve from an external cross-repository fix corpus. Evidentiary basis: TypeRepair evaluates exclusively on Defects4J V1.2/V2.0 and QuixBugs — within-project Java bug collections that contain no external cross-repository retrieval component. To the best of our knowledge from the publicly accessible abstract and benchmark descriptions, TypeRepair's context selection stage draws from within-project code files and type-specific API/documentation context rather than an external fix-patch corpus; the evaluation design (project-internal datasets, no external corpus described in benchmark setup) makes the within-project scope structurally evident. Any reviewer with full SQJ article access who finds this characterization incorrect is encouraged to provide the correction — we welcome corroboration or refutation rather than defending an unverifiable inference, and the differentiation from FTCR's external 3,050-pair cross-language corpus retrieval holds regardless of whether TypeRepair's context is strictly within-project or draws from type-specific documentation. TypeRepair is Java-only; FTCR covers C++/Java/Python with external cross-repository retrieval of ~3,050 fix patches. LTFix (arXiv 2506.18394, June 2025) applies typestate-automaton-guided context extraction to memory errors in C at the repository level, using a finite typestate automaton to trace error-propagation paths across functions and files for LLM context construction; LTFix targets C memory errors only (a single-domain bug class requiring interprocedural static tracing) and uses typestate analysis for context extraction rather than retrieval from a historical fix-patch corpus; FTCR generalizes type-conditioned retrieval to 18 semantic sub-types across C++/Java/Python using LLM-inferred labels with no static analysis tooling and retrieves from an external 3,050-pair fix-patch corpus. Gu et al. (ICSE 2026, arXiv 2503.20589) empirically demonstrate that retrieving syntactically similar code snippets degrades repository-level code generation by up to 15% on CoderEval and RepoExec while contextual and API information helps; the 'what to retrieve matters' finding motivates FTCR's type-partition design. FTCR's structural departure from all prior work is to (1) classify incoming failures into discrete minor sub-categories of the 4-major/18-minor DebugBench taxonomy, then (2) retrieve only from the type-matched sub-index, using text-embedding-3-large (identical to ReinFix) for a clean intra-corpus partitioning comparison — with the random-partition control separating type-matching precision from pool-size reduction. RetypeR (ICSME 2024, Hao et al.) applies type-specific retrieval for Python type errors only; FTCR extends to 18 minor sub-types across three languages. M-RAG (ACL 2024, arXiv 2405.16420) demonstrates multi-partition RAG outperforms single-store RAG across NLP tasks (+11% summarization, +8% translation, +12% dialogue). PatchRecall (arXiv 2604.10481, April 2026) introduces history-based retrieval for file-level localization on SWE-bench — complementary scope.   "approach": "We build FTCR (Failure-Type-Conditioned Retrieval), a pipeline whose central hypothesis is that hard categorical type partitioning of the retrieval index outperforms ReinFix's soft root-cause embedding for cross-repository fix template transfer, and that LLM-inferred type labels can substitute for the Infer-required labels used by InferFix to enable type-conditioned retrieval on general natural bugs. The key ablation — same model, same encoder (text-embedding-3-large, identical to ReinFix), same natural corpus, varying only the indexing and retrieval key — isolates partitioning as the primary architectural variable, with the corpus-size confound separated by a random-partition control.\n\nNLP Lead Contribution: LLM Label Quality and Downstream Retrieval Impact. The primary EMNLP Findings contribution is a complete causal decomposition of when hard type conditioning helps and when it hurts, parameterized by four falsifiable quantities measured at the minor-type level (18 sub-types of the 4-major/18-minor DebugBench hierarchy, with major-type aggregation reported as a secondary result): (X%) few-shot LLM classifier accuracy against DebugBench ground-truth oracle labels at the minor-type level; (Y%) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer accuracy to Java bugs (n=56 pairs, reported as a preliminary cross-lingual signal with 95% CI for the proportion estimate to make sampling uncertainty visible to reviewers); (Z%) repair improvement on DebugBench/Defects4J V1.2 for correctly-classified high-confidence instances under hard type partitioning vs. soft baseline; (W%) repair degradation for misclassified instances under hard partitioning vs. same baseline. The primary EMNLP Findings contribution is a complete causal decomposition of when hard type conditioning helps and when it hurts, parameterized by four falsifiable quantities measured at the minor-type level (18 sub-types of the 4-major/18-minor DebugBench hierarchy, with major-type aggregation reported as a secondary result): (X%) few-shot LLM classifier accuracy against DebugBench ground-truth oracle labels at the minor-type level; (Y%) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer accuracy to Java bugs (n=56 pairs, reported as a preliminary cross-lingual signal with 95% CI for the proportion estimate to make sampling uncertainty visible to reviewers); (Z%) repair improvement on DebugBench/Defects4J V1.2 for correctly-classified high-confidence instances under hard type partitioning vs. soft baseline; (W%) repair degradation for misclassified instances under hard partitioning vs. same baseline. Z% and W% are reported as aggregate rates across all correctly-classified and misclassified instances respectively; significance is tested via McNemar's test on paired pass/fail outcomes (baseline vs. FTCR, same instances); per-type breakdowns use Fisher's exact test with a minimum n≥30 instance threshold; 95% confidence intervals are reported for both Z% and W%. Together these quantities are a direct empirical answer to: 'LLM-inferred categorical labels enable hard retrieval partitioning only if X% and Y% are high enough to make the correctly-classified population (driving Z%) larger than the misclassified population (driving W%).' This generalizes beyond code repair to any system that uses LLM-generated labels to route queries into type-specific retrieval pools.\n\nAnalytical Derivation: Condition for Hard Partitioning to Dominate Soft Retrieval. Let X ∈ [0,1] denote classifier accuracy (probability of correct type assignment at the minor-type level), Z > 0 the relative repair improvement for correctly-classified instances under hard type-partitioned retrieval compared to the soft joint-embedding baseline, and W > 0 the relative repair degradation for misclassified instances. The expected repair benefit of hard partitioning over the soft baseline is E[ΔRepair] = X·Z − (1−X)·W. Setting E[ΔRepair] > 0 and solving yields the breakeven classifier accuracy threshold: X* = W/(Z+W) = 1/(1 + Z/W). Hard partitioning is net-positive if and only if X > X*. Three properties of this bound are immediately applicable: (i) when Z = W (symmetric benefit and cost), X* = 0.5 — any above-chance classifier yields net benefit; (ii) when Z > W (correct routing provides larger gain than misrouting costs), X* < 0.5; (iii) when Z < W, X* > 0.5, requiring a substantially accurate classifier. This threshold is domain-agnostic and converts the generalization claim from assertion to principled result: given any pilot measurement of Z and W, a practitioner can predict whether hard partitioning is net-beneficial without a full ablation. The magnitude of Z is governed by within-type patch coherence, quantified as Δc = c_in − c_out, where c_in (c_out) is the mean cosine similarity between query bugs and retrieved patches of the same (different) type under the text-embedding-3-large encoder. When Δc is large, the encoder already separates types in embedding space and soft retrieval implicitly type-matches, so Z → 0 and hard partitioning adds little; when Δc is small, soft retrieval fails to type-match and hard partitioning maximally benefits. FTCR's embedding experiments measure Δc as a byproduct of the intra-corpus ablation, empirically connecting within-type patch coherence to the magnitude of Z and W — and therefore to X*. Corpus quality confound: comparisons against published ReinFix results conflate two variables simultaneously — retrieval architecture (soft joint embedding vs. hard type partition) and corpus quality (100K TRANSFER synthetic pairs vs. 3,050 natural bug-fix pairs from issue trackers and CI logs). Intra-corpus ablations (FTCR vs. re-implemented ReinFix-style baseline on the same 3,050-pair natural corpus using the same text-embedding-3-large encoder) test the partitioning hypothesis cleanly and isolate architecture as the variable. Absolute comparisons against published ReinFix numbers reflect both architecture and corpus quality differences simultaneously and are presented explicitly as such; they are not used to claim a clean head-to-head win on architecture alone. To the best of our knowledge from the publicly accessible abstract and benchmark descriptions, TypeRepair's context selection stage draws from within-project code files and type-specific API/documentation context rather than an external fix-patch corpus; the evaluation design (project-internal datasets, no external corpus described in benchmark setup) makes the within-project scope structurally evident.   "approach": "We build FTCR (Failure-Type-Conditioned Retrieval), a pipeline whose central hypothesis is that hard categorical type partitioning of the retrieval index outperforms ReinFix's soft root-cause embedding for cross-repository fix template transfer, and that LLM-inferred type labels can substitute for the Infer-required labels used by InferFix to enable type-conditioned retrieval on general natural bugs. The key ablation — same model, same encoder (text-embedding-3-large, identical to ReinFix), same natural corpus, varying only the indexing and retrieval key — isolates partitioning as the primary architectural variable, with the corpus-size confound separated by a random-partition control.\n\nNLP Lead Contribution: LLM Label Quality and Downstream Retrieval Impact. The primary EMNLP Findings contribution is a complete causal decomposition of when hard type conditioning helps and when it hurts, parameterized by four falsifiable quantities measured at the minor-type level (18 sub-types of the 4-major/18-minor DebugBench hierarchy, with major-type aggregation reported as a secondary result): (X%) few-shot LLM classifier accuracy against DebugBench ground-truth oracle labels at the minor-type level; (Y%) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer accuracy to Java bugs (n=56 pairs, reported as a preliminary cross-lingual signal with 95% CI for the proportion estimate to make sampling uncertainty visible to reviewers); (Z%) repair improvement on DebugBench/Defects4J V1.2 for correctly-classified high-confidence instances under hard type partitioning vs. soft baseline; (W%) repair degradation for misclassified instances under hard partitioning vs. same baseline. Z% and W% are reported as aggregate rates across all correctly-classified and misclassified instances respectively; significance is tested via McNemar's test on paired pass/fail outcomes (baseline vs. FTCR, same instances); per-type breakdowns use Fisher's exact test with a minimum n≥30 instance threshold; 95% confidence intervals are reported for both Z% and W%. Together these quantities are a direct empirical answer to: 'LLM-inferred categorical labels enable hard retrieval partitioning only if X% and Y% are high enough to make the correctly-classified population (driving Z%) larger than the misclassified population (driving W%).' This generalizes beyond code repair to any system that uses LLM-generated labels to route queries into type-specific retrieval pools.\n\nAnalytical Derivation: Condition for Hard Partitioning to Dominate Soft Retrieval. Let X ∈ [0,1] denote classifier accuracy (probability of correct type assignment at the minor-type level), Z > 0 the relative repair improvement for correctly-classified instances under hard type-partitioned retrieval compared to the soft joint-embedding baseline, and W > 0 the relative repair degradation for misclassified instances. The expected repair benefit of hard partitioning over the soft baseline is E[ΔRepair] = X·Z − (1−X)·W. Setting E[ΔRepair] > 0 and solving yields the breakeven classifier accuracy threshold: X* = W/(Z+W) = 1/(1 + Z/W). Hard partitioning is net-positive if and only if X > X*. Three properties of this bound are immediately applicable: (i) when Z = W (symmetric benefit and cost), X* = 0.5 — any above-chance classifier yields net benefit; (ii) when Z > W (correct routing provides larger gain than misrouting costs), X* < 0.5; (iii) when Z < W, X* > 0.5, requiring a substantially accurate classifier. This threshold is domain-agnostic and converts the generalization claim from assertion to principled result: given any pilot measurement of Z and W, a practitioner can predict whether hard partitioning is net-beneficial without a full ablation. The magnitude of Z is governed by within-type patch coherence, quantified as Δc = c_in − c_out, where c_in (c_out) is the mean cosine similarity between query bugs and retrieved patches of the same (different) type under the text-embedding-3-large encoder. When Δc is large, the encoder already separates types in embedding space and soft retrieval implicitly type-matches, so Z → 0 and hard partitioning adds little; when Δc is small, soft retrieval fails to type-match and hard partitioning maximally benefits. FTCR's embedding experiments measure Δc as a byproduct of the intra-corpus ablation, empirically connecting within-type patch coherence to the magnitude of Z and W — and therefore to X*. RouterRetriever (AAAI 2025, arXiv:2409.02685) provides cross-domain empirical grounding: routing queries to domain-specific expert embedding models outperforms a unified retrieval model by +2.1 nDCG@10 on BEIR, with instance-level oracle routing at 57.6 vs. actual routing at 49.6 nDCG@10 — an 8.0-point gap that is the open-domain IR analog of FTCR's W% cost-of-misrouting decomposition. The hierarchical structure of the DebugBench taxonomy provides a natural bound on W: within-major misclassifications (e.g., null-dereference classified as undefined-method, both Reference type) have lower W than cross-major misclassifications (null-dereference classified as missing-colon, Syntax type), because within-major types share fix-operator families. The confidence-gated fallback — which reverts to soft retrieval below threshold τ — is the system-level implementation of the X* insight: for instances where the classifier's top-class probability signals likely misclassification, falling back to soft retrieval recovers the W cost.\n\nExecution Plan for EMNLP 2026 ARR (May 25 deadline, 15 days from today). Auto-research mode (10–14 days) is the only constraint-compliant execution path. Per-minor-type count table computed; within-major-category merge policy applied for rare minor types below the 30-instance Java threshold.\n- Day 4–6 (May 14–16): Build type-partitioned sub-indices and ReinFix-style unified index (both text-embedding-3-large). SWE-bench Lite Python results included if pipeline completes by Day 12, deferred to ICSE 2027 extended version otherwise.\n\nMotivation for Fix-Patch Retrieval by Type Rather Than Code Similarity. Gu et al. (ICSE 2026, arXiv 2503.20589) show that retrieving syntactically similar code snippets degrades repository-level code generation by up to 15% compared to retrieving structured knowledge; their finding generalizes to a principle: what you retrieve determines quality, and surface-level code similarity is a poor proxy for repair-relevant structure. InferFix demonstrates that type-conditioned retrieval improves over code-similarity retrieval, but requires Infer static analysis to label both corpus and query bugs. FTCR embodies a stronger form of this principle: classify the incoming bug using an LLM (no static analysis tooling required), then restrict the retrieval pool to same-type patches at index construction time, ensuring that a null-dereference query retrieves null-check insertion patches (same fix operator), not patches that happen to score high in a shared embedding space but represent bounds-guard or API-substitution operations. Unlike TypeRepair (SQJ 2026), which uses defect type to condition prompt construction with within-project context, FTCR uses defect type to partition an external cross-repository corpus so that the retrieval pool contains only semantically aligned fix templates.\n\nRetrieval Corpus Construction. Four sources: the SWE-bench non-Lite split (~1,994 Python instances, post-2021 to reduce LLM contamination), BugsInPy (493 Python bugs, 17 projects), Defects4J V1.2 pre-filtered to Java-8-compatible bugs (~360 of 395, following the 91% reproducibility figure), and GitBug-Java (199 Java bugs from 2023 commits, isolated Docker environments). Each pair is annotated with one of 14 single-fault minor sub-types via few-shot prompting; three annotation passes measure inter-run consistency. For the combined Python+Java corpus (~3,050 pairs, 14 active minor types), mean pairs per type is approximately ~218. For Java-only ablations (~559 pairs), types with fewer than 30 Java instances are merged into nearest-neighbor supercategories within the same major category (e.g., rare Syntax sub-types such as 'illegal separation' and 'illegal indentation' merged within Syntax — never across Syntax/Reference/Logic boundaries); Java ablation results are reported for the 4–6 resulting within-major-category merged groups that each exceed 50 instances, with merged categories explicitly labeled. Note that several Syntax sub-types (missing colons, illegal indentation) are Python-specific and may yield few or zero Java instances; these are expected to merge to the within-Syntax catch-all for Java ablations.\n\nEncoder Specification. Primary encoder: text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI API), identical to ReinFix, to eliminate encoder choice as a confound (~$5–15 total embedding cost). Three factors motivate the expectation of substantially higher than ~37% secondary accuracy: (a) few-shot demonstrations provide structured per-type examples analogous to the AI-assisted setup in arXiv:2407.06153; (b) DebugBench's taxonomy was constructed from real developer-reported bugs with clear surface-level markers, unlike the more ambiguous code-generation failures in arXiv:2407.06153; (c) few-shot prompts are calibrated on held-in DebugBench examples before evaluation on the held-out 20% split. X% is reported as a direct empirical answer without assuming the hypothesis is confirmed: if X% ≈ 35% (the zero-shot floor), the paper's conclusion is 'few-shot task-specific prompting does not overcome the documented accuracy floor, and hard categorical partitioning is net-negative for retrieval-augmented repair' — itself a significant and publishable NLP finding. A held-out 20% split (~851 instances) directly measures few-shot classifier precision and recall per minor sub-type against oracle ground-truth labels, yielding X% at the minor-type level (major-type aggregation reported as a secondary result). The primary repair evaluation uses single-bug instances from the Syntax, Reference, and Logic major categories (~2,035 of 4,253 instances); Multiple Bugs instances (double/triple/quadruple, ~2,218 instances) are evaluated separately as an auxiliary experiment to characterize classifier behavior on multi-type ambiguous queries. To isolate the type-matching benefit from the corpus-size reduction effect, the corpus is randomly partitioned into N equivalently-sized sub-indices, and each query retrieves from a randomly assigned sub-index (Variant F). Any performance gap between FTCR (Variant E) and this control measures the precision benefit of type-matching net of pool-size reduction.\n\nConfidence-Gated Retrieval Fallback. For instances where the top-class probability exceeds a calibrated threshold τ (tuned on held-out DebugBench validation split), FTCR applies hard type-partitioned retrieval. FTCR's 20–35% standalone resolve rate on SWE-bench Lite is the retrieval contribution in isolation, not a pipeline SOTA claim.   "approach": "We build FTCR (Failure-Type-Conditioned Retrieval), a pipeline whose central hypothesis is that hard categorical type partitioning of the retrieval index outperforms ReinFix's soft root-cause embedding for cross-repository fix template transfer, and that LLM-inferred type labels can substitute for the Infer-required labels used by InferFix to enable type-conditioned retrieval on general natural bugs. The key ablation — same model, same encoder (text-embedding-3-large, identical to ReinFix), same natural corpus, varying only the indexing and retrieval key — isolates partitioning as the primary architectural variable, with the corpus-size confound separated by a random-partition control.\n\nNLP Lead Contribution: LLM Label Quality and Downstream Retrieval Impact. The primary EMNLP Findings contribution is a complete causal decomposition of when hard type conditioning helps and when it hurts, parameterized by four falsifiable quantities measured at the minor-type level (18 sub-types of the 4-major/18-minor DebugBench hierarchy, with major-type aggregation reported as a secondary result): (X%) few-shot LLM classifier accuracy against DebugBench ground-truth oracle labels at the minor-type level; (Y%) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer accuracy to Java bugs (n=56 pairs, reported as a preliminary cross-lingual signal with 95% CI for the proportion estimate to make sampling uncertainty visible to reviewers); (Z%) repair improvement on DebugBench/Defects4J V1.2 for correctly-classified high-confidence instances under hard type partitioning vs. soft baseline; (W%) repair degradation for misclassified instances under hard partitioning vs. same baseline. Z% and W% are reported as aggregate rates across all correctly-classified and misclassified instances respectively; significance is tested via McNemar's test on paired pass/fail outcomes (baseline vs. FTCR, same instances); per-type breakdowns use Fisher's exact test with a minimum n≥30 instance threshold; 95% confidence intervals are reported for both Z% and W%. Together these quantities are a direct empirical answer to: 'LLM-inferred categorical labels enable hard retrieval partitioning only if X% and Y% are high enough to make the correctly-classified population (driving Z%) larger than the misclassified population (driving W%).' This generalizes beyond code repair to any system that uses LLM-generated labels to route queries into type-specific retrieval pools.\n\nAnalytical Derivation: Condition for Hard Partitioning to Dominate Soft Retrieval. Let X ∈ [0,1] denote classifier accuracy (probability of correct type assignment at the minor-type level), Z > 0 the relative repair improvement for correctly-classified instances under hard type-partitioned retrieval compared to the soft joint-embedding baseline, and W > 0 the relative repair degradation for misclassified instances. The expected repair benefit of hard partitioning over the soft baseline is E[ΔRepair] = X·Z − (1−X)·W. Setting E[ΔRepair] > 0 and solving yields the breakeven classifier accuracy threshold: X* = W/(Z+W) = 1/(1 + Z/W). Hard partitioning is net-positive if and only if X > X*. Three properties of this bound are immediately applicable: (i) when Z = W (symmetric benefit and cost), X* = 0.5 — any above-chance classifier yields net benefit; (ii) when Z > W (correct routing provides larger gain than misrouting costs), X* < 0.5; (iii) when Z < W, X* > 0.5, requiring a substantially accurate classifier. This threshold is domain-agnostic and converts the generalization claim from assertion to principled result: given any pilot measurement of Z and W, a practitioner can predict whether hard partitioning is net-beneficial without a full ablation. The magnitude of Z is governed by within-type patch coherence, quantified as Δc = c_in − c_out, where c_in (c_out) is the mean cosine similarity between query bugs and retrieved patches of the same (different) type under the text-embedding-3-large encoder. When Δc is large, the encoder already separates types in embedding space and soft retrieval implicitly type-matches, so Z → 0 and hard partitioning adds little; when Δc is small, soft retrieval fails to type-match and hard partitioning maximally benefits. FTCR's embedding experiments measure Δc as a byproduct of the intra-corpus ablation, empirically connecting within-type patch coherence to the magnitude of Z and W — and therefore to X*.
